dimensions.label: Type
dimensions.asks: can the language keep the *meaning of a value* in one place, or must every reader reconstruct it?

dimensions.label: Construction
dimensions.asks: can the language keep state local, and can a value only come into existence through a path that establishes its invariant?

dimensions.label: Memory
dimensions.asks: can the language state when storage and other resources are released, and who owns them?

dimensions.label: Error
dimensions.asks: can a failure travel from where it is detected to where it can be handled, and does anything require a caller to decide?

dimensions.label: Concurrency
dimensions.asks: can the language express parallel work, and can it keep that work from touching shared state unintentionally?

dimensions.label: Platform
dimensions.asks: can the artifact run anywhere other than where it was built for?

dimensions.label: Performance
dimensions.asks: is there a cost the program pays at run time that its source does not show?

dimensions.label: Ecosystem
dimensions.asks: does the surrounding supply of libraries, tools, and people make the language's own costs worse?

dimensions.label: Evolution
dimensions.asks: will the code still mean what it means after the language moves?

dimensions.label: Domain
dimensions.asks: is the language shaped for one target so tightly that adopting it means adopting that target?

dimensions.label: Learning
dimensions.asks: what does a practitioner pay to become productive, and who bears that cost?

dimensions.label: Syntax
dimensions.asks: how much of the reader's attention does the notation itself consume?

dimensions.label: Testing
dimensions.asks: how does the language help the program find its own mistakes, and how much of that work is left to the team?

dimensions.label: Security
dimensions.asks: does the language make a whole class of exploit possible, or a whole class of mistake silent?

dimensions.label: Reproducibility
dimensions.asks: can you rebuild the artifact and get the same thing?

dimensions.label: Supply chain
dimensions.asks: can you verify what you shipped?

dimensions.label: Observability
dimensions.asks: can you see what the program does in production?

dimensions.label: Feedback
dimensions.asks: how fast is the edit-build-test loop?

dimensions.label: Interop
dimensions.asks: can the language work with code written in another language?

dimensions.label: Governance
dimensions.asks: will the language be maintained, and by whom?

criteria.text: A value carries its type at run time, so nothing checks that an operation suits its operand until the operation runs. The meaning of every value becomes a shared agreement between the site that produces it and every site that consumes it, and no tool holds that agreement: it lives in the tests and in the reader's memory.

Type-identity coupling across the whole program: producer and consumer agree on what a value *is*, and on every operation that may apply to it, and nothing in the source records that agreement. Because the check happens when the operation runs, the agreement survives only while both sides are read together, so a change to one reaches all the others at once.

Python accepts `n = 1` and then `n = "one"`, and `n + 1` fails only on the path that reaches it, and only for the inputs that take that path. MATLAB, R, SAS, Lua, and every POSIX shell behave the same way.

**Presence does not mean a checker is unavailable.** The criterion asks whether the language *enforces* a check. A program that runs `mypy --strict` in CI has a check the language did not give it, and the score still records the language.

The compiler knows the types, but it converts between them implicitly, so a check that would catch a mistake becomes a silent conversion. The conversion rules become the shared resource: every expression depends on a table that nothing forces a reader to know.

Conversion coupling: every expression that mixes types agrees with the language's conversion table rather than with its neighbour. The table is the shared resource, so a reader who does not hold it cannot tell a checked expression from a silently narrowed one, and an implicit conversion hides the moment the meaning changed.

C compiles `int i = 3.7;` and discards the fraction, and lets an integer stand in for a pointer. COBOL converts between two different `PICTURE` clauses on a `MOVE` without complaint. Visual Basic's `Option Strict Off` default admits a narrowing conversion and a late-bound call.

Which code a call reaches is decided by the value's run-time type rather than by a declared contract. The set of operations a value must answer becomes a shared agreement that no declaration holds, so a rename in one module breaks a caller in another — and only at run time.

Call-target coupling: a caller and a callee agree on a name and an arity that no declaration enforces, and the agreement must hold for every type that can arrive at the call site. Because the target is chosen from the value, the coupling spans types the author of the call never named.

Erlang resolves `Mod:Fun(Args)` when it is called, so a missing function fails there; Elixir and Clojure choose a protocol or a pattern clause from the value they receive; Ruby and Python resolve an attribute at the moment of the call.

**Presence does not mean `T1`.** Objective-C is statically typed at the pointer level and still dispatches every message at run time, so it is charged `T3` and not `T1`. TypeScript is statically typed and still reaches a method through the prototype at run time, so it is charged the same way. Duck typing is about *which code runs*; `T1` is about *what a value is*.

The language cannot declare that a value is one of several alternatives and have the compiler track which one. The alternatives are encoded by convention, so the tag and its payload are a shared resource that every consumer re-derives, and the compiler cannot prove that a consumer handles every case.

Encoding coupling: producer and consumer agree on how an alternative is written down — a tag beside a payload, a `nil`, a nullable column — rather than on the alternative itself. The encoding is the shared resource, so a new case has to be taught to every reader of it, and exhaustiveness stays a convention.

Go has no sum type, so "a value or a failure" is a pair and a `nil` check stands in for a match. SQL models an alternative as nullable columns, and the caller must know the encoding. Rust's `enum` and C++'s `std::variant` are the constructs whose absence is charged.
**Minor because it is containable.** A constructor plus its accessors can confine the cost to one place — but never to zero, because exhaustiveness stays unchecked.

The language cannot write an algorithm once over a type parameter, so it duplicates the code per type or falls back on one universal representation. That representation becomes the shared resource, and every user casts out of it, so the type is known by convention.

Representation coupling: every use of the algorithm agrees on the one representation it can carry — `void *`, `Object`, `interface{}` — and casts back out by hand. The universal representation is the shared resource, so the real type of a value becomes knowledge held by the programmer rather than a fact held by the compiler.

Pre-generics Java needed `(String) list.get(0)` from an `Object` container; C passes `void *` with a callback; Go before 1.18 used `interface{}`; SQL has no type parameter at all and generates DDL per column type instead.

**Presence does not mean the *checking* half of generics.** A language with generics whose parameters cannot be constrained still leaves a gap — but that gap is charged under `T2` or `T3`. `T5` records only the absence of the type parameter itself.

The language has a single flat name space, so two declarations with the same name collide whichever module they live in. The global name space is the clearest shared resource there is: every name is a claim on it, and a new module can break an unrelated one.

Name coupling over one flat space: every declaration competes for the same set of identifiers, so two modules that never call each other are coupled through the name they both want. The name space is the shared resource, and nothing local bounds a claim on it, which is why the convention that resolves it — a prefix — must be kept by the whole codebase.

Two C libraries that both define `init` cannot be linked without renaming one, which is why C libraries prefix their symbols (`gl_`, `png_`). Lua keeps every global in one shared table. An assembler puts every global symbol in one flat symbol table.

**Presence asks about the mechanism, not the idiom.** MATLAB is not charged, because `+pkg` folders scope a name, and R is not charged, because a package declares a `NAMESPACE`. C is charged, because a header's declarations all land in one translator-level name space.

The type parameter is present in the source and gone from the artifact, and the program can inspect and alter its own structure at run time. The erased type is a shared resource that no longer travels with the value, so a consumer must recover it by convention — and reflection turns every private field into a reachable one.

Type-recovery coupling at the boundary: the consumer agrees with the producer on a type argument that the artifact no longer carries. The agreement sits where the cast is written, so it holds per call site and cannot be checked back at the place the value was made.

Java's `List<String>` is a `List` at run time, so `get(0)` returns `Object` and the cast is unchecked. Objective-C's `id` carries no compile-time type at all. TypeScript's types exist in the editor and the build, and not in the running program.
**Minor because the cost sits at the boundary** where the type is recovered — a cast, a `Class<T>` token, an `isKindOfClass:` test — not in the body of the algorithm.

A symbol such as `+`, `==`, or `[]` takes its meaning from the operand types. A symbol is a shared resource with one meaning by default, and overloading makes that meaning depend on a lookup the reader has to perform.

Symbol-meaning coupling: the reader agrees with the definer on what `+` or `==` does for the type at hand. The meaning is resolved by a lookup at the use, so the coupling is real but bounded to one expression — the reader resolves one type and the answer arrives.
C++'s `<<` both shifts and inserts into a stream. Scala's `+` on a `Set` performs a union. Racket's `+` accepts exact and inexact numbers and returns whichever type the operands dictate.
**Minor because the operator still carries a type signature**, so its meaning is discoverable by resolving one type — unlike a macro, which can mean anything at all.

The only way to use two types through one interface is to place both in an inheritance chain. The base type becomes a shared resource that the types must be *placed into*, which forces an "is-a" commitment wherever the domain has only "does-this", and a change to the base changes every subtype.

Hierarchy coupling: a type agrees to be *placed under* the interface it will be used through, so it inherits its base's identity and its base's future changes. The chain is the shared resource, so a change at the root reaches every leaf, and an unrelated type must be moved into the chain before it can play the role.

Eiffel's polymorphism runs through its inheritance and genericity rules. C approximates it with a `struct` holding function pointers, or with a `void *` and a convention. TclOO expresses a shared protocol as a class or a mixin rather than a declared type.
**Minor, and the cheapest to remove.** Go's implicit interfaces, Rust's traits, and Elixir's protocols supply polymorphism without a chain, so those languages are not charged.

Any reference can be the absent value, and nothing in the type says whether it is. "May be absent" becomes a shared resource that every consumer must guard, and no signature records the guard, so each reader repeats the check or forgets it.

Absence coupling: every consumer agrees with every producer about whether a reference may be missing, and no signature records the answer. The unwritten agreement is the shared resource, so each guard is written per use and each omission stays invisible until the missing value arrives.

Java compiles `String s = null; s.length()`. SQL's `NULL` is compatible with every domain and propagates through three-valued logic, so `IF x = 5` is not true when `x` is `NULL`. In PL/SQL a variable that is never assigned is `NULL`. A null pointer in Assembly is a zero register, and a load from it is an ordinary instruction.

**Presence does not mean "the language has an absent value".** Kotlin's `String?` against `String`, Swift's optionals, Rust's `Option<T>`, and TypeScript's `string | null` under `strict` are exactly the construct whose absence is charged, which is why those languages are not charged `T10`.

There is no construct that declares what a module exposes and what it keeps. The boundary is the shared resource, and its absence means every declaration is reachable by every consumer, so an internal change can break an unrelated caller.

Visibility coupling in its total form: every declaration is a public fact, so a consumer may depend on anything a producer contains. The missing boundary is what makes the coupling unbounded — a change to an internal name travels to callers the module never intended to have.

A C header makes everything it declares public, and `static` is the only file-scoped boundary. A POSIX shell script sources another script into the same variable space. VBScript's `ExecuteGlobal` writes into the same global scope. Scratch exposes every sprite's blocks with no declared interface.

**Presence does not mean "no files".** Splitting code across files is not a boundary. Go is not charged, because a package-level unexported name is a real boundary, and neither is MATLAB, whose `+pkg` and `private` folders hide what they do not export.

A call's signature says what it returns, not what it does. The effects a call may perform — input and output, mutation of shared state, exceptions, randomness — are a shared resource that no declaration carries, so every caller learns them by reading the body or by testing. A change to an effect is invisible to every caller [@brachthauser2020effects].

Effect coupling: a caller agrees with a callee on what the call may *do*, and reads that agreement from the body rather than from the signature. Because the effect set is unwritten, every caller is exposed to every effect the implementation may later acquire.

Haskell's `IO`, PureScript's `Effect`, and Unison's abilities put the effects in the type, so a function cannot hide a socket behind a pure signature. In Java, Python, Go, and C a function that writes a file, mutates a global, and throws looks like any other function.

**Held at Moderate, not High.** The breadth is the whole program — any call may perform any effect — but nothing breaks when the effect set is wrong. The cost is the reading and refactoring work an untracked effect adds, not a missed check, so the mechanism does not carry a High mechanism's weight.

**Presence records whether the type states the effects.** Every language has effects. Haskell, PureScript, Unison, Lean 4, and Rocq carry them in the type; so do Nim (its `raises` and `tags` lists are part of a proc type) and D (`pure`, `nothrow`, and `@nogc` are constituents of the function type). Java's `throws` clause is a signature annotation, not part of the method type, so Java is charged.

The language has two kinds of function — one that may suspend and one that may not — and the two do not compose. A synchronous function cannot call an asynchronous one without a bridge, so the kind spreads outward through the call graph and every caller must agree on it. The kind is a shared resource that a change in one function imposes on the whole chain [@nystrom2015color].

Function-kind coupling along the call chain: a caller must share the kind of its callee, so the kind propagates from the smallest suspending leaf to the entry point. The kind is the shared resource, so adopting it at one site is a decision that the whole chain must repeat.
**Presence records a function-kind split**, not the existence of concurrency. Go's goroutines and Erlang's processes are concurrency without a second function kind, so neither is charged.

In JavaScript, C#, and Dart an `async` function returns a future, and a plain function that calls it must itself become `async` or block. Rust's `async fn` returns a `Future` that only an executor drives, Nim's `{.async.}` proc can be awaited only inside another async proc, and Python's `async def` and Kotlin's `suspend` draw the same line.

The language can call code outside its own type system, and nothing checks that the two sides agree. The foreign interface — argument order, ownership, layout, lifetime, and error convention — is a shared resource held by a hand-written declaration, so a mismatch is found at run time or not at all.

ABI coupling at the foreign boundary: the two sides agree on argument order, layout, ownership, and error convention through a hand-written declaration that neither compiler validates. The declaration is the shared resource, so the agreement holds until run time and then fails as corruption rather than as a diagnostic.

Rust's `extern "C"` block is an unchecked promise. Python's `ctypes` and Ruby's `Fiddle` accept any signature. JNI requires the C side to agree by hand, and a Java exception that crosses the boundary unwinds nothing on the other side.
**Minor because the boundary is containable to one module** — but never zero, because the compiler cannot check across it.

**Covers the native boundary, not a boundary inside one runtime.** Unison 1.0 added a C FFI, so it is charged. PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server can load native code through a user-defined function, so the procedural SQL dialects are charged with them. Solidity calls only inside the EVM, and a shell reaches foreign code by starting a process, so neither is charged. The readiness axis prices the other side of the same boundary, under `Y9`: a language is charged there for having no interface, and here for the interface being unchecked. Both can be charged at once.

The default home for a value is a global that any code can read and write; state is local only when the programmer asks for it. The global is the widest shared resource there is — the whole program is its consumer — so any module can change it, and any change can surprise any reader.

State coupling to one cell: every reader and every writer of the global agrees on its meaning at each instant, and the whole program is a party to that agreement. Because the cell has no owner, no module can change its own behaviour without the possibility of changing another's.

Python's module-level names and `global`. MATLAB's base workspace, and R's global environment with `<<-`. A POSIX shell, where `x=1` inside a function can write the caller's variable. COBOL's `WORKING-STORAGE`. A PL/SQL package variable, which lives for the whole session.
**Presence asks whether a global is the *default*.** Every language permits a global. Kotlin and Rust make top-level state immutable unless it is declared otherwise, so neither is charged.
A binding, and the value behind it, can be changed unless the programmer says otherwise. "Who may write this?" then has no default answer, so every reader has to trace the writes.

Write-permission coupling: every holder of a binding must know which other holders may change it, and the language states no default answer. The permissive default makes the coupling silent at the definition and forces it to be reconstructed at every read.
Java fields are mutable unless they are `final`; C++ members unless they are `const`; a MATLAB array is mutable with no `const` at all; a SAS DATA step may overwrite the dataset it is reading.
**Minor because immutability is usually a local decision.** A language that inverts the default — Rust's `let` with `mut`, Haskell's bindings — is not charged.

Creating a value and obtaining its storage are one act, and the construction cannot be redirected to different storage. The storage site becomes a shared resource, so a caller cannot choose where a value lives, and the code that builds a value cannot be separated from the code that reserves it.

Storage coupling: the constructor and the caller must agree on where the value will live, because the language offers no way to separate the act of construction from the act of reservation. The agreement is narrow — one allocation site — which is why a single indirection removes it.

In C a value exists only because storage was reserved and then filled, and a constructor is a naming convention over `malloc`. In Assembly the reservation is a register or a stack slot, and nothing constructs.

**Minor because one indirection restores the separation.** C++'s placement construction and allocator-aware containers, and Rust's `Box` and `Vec::with_capacity`, build in storage that already exists, so those languages are not charged.
A value of the type can exist without having passed any validating path. The invariant becomes a shared resource that nothing enforces, so every consumer either re-validates or simply trusts.

Invariant coupling: every consumer must agree with every producer that a value is valid, because no constructor stands between the type and its instances. The agreement is silent — a consumer cannot tell a validated value from an unvalidated one.

A C `struct` is uninitialized memory until each field is assigned. A Fortran variable can be referenced before it is set. A Solidity contract without a `constructor` is deployed with whatever the default state is. In a POSIX shell a variable comes into existence on first assignment, and no construct can state an invariant about it.
**Minor because the invariant can often be re-established cheaply** — a smart constructor, a factory, a private field plus a validating entry point. The criterion is the same either way.

mechanisms.label: unpinned collection order
mechanisms.title: Iteration Order Is the Data Structure's, Not the Source's

criteria.text: The key-value container the source uses iterates in an order the source does not state: the specification leaves map iteration unspecified, and the default type in the shipped library is the unordered one. Code that assembles output, report text, a serialized payload, or a join order from an iteration is agreeing with a hash function. Go and Rust randomize the order between runs on purpose, Perl randomizes it to catch the agreement, Scala switches from insertion order to hashed order when the fifth entry arrives — documented, and silent.

Order coupling at iteration sites: the sequence of a traversal is a shared resource between the container's internals and every consumer of its order. The source cannot pin it, the type does not name it, and a change to a key set, a capacity, or a seed moves the output of a program nobody changed. The fix is a discipline — choose the ordered container, sort the keys, never rely on the order — and a discipline is what the model prices as present.

The Java specification states the iteration order of HashMap need not be constant; the Go specification states map iteration receives no order guarantee, and the runtime randomizes the seed each run; Rust's HashMap documents the per-process random seed; Perl's documentation states the hash order is the implementation's and varies; Lua's reference says pairs() walks in an order 'decided by the internal data structures'; the CLHS states hash iteration is unspecified; Swift documents Dictionary order as 'not specified'; Microsoft documents Dictionary order as not to be relied on.

**`V5` prices a default that drifts; this prices an order the source never owned.** `V5` charges a build-time default changing between releases; `C5` charges a run-time order not pinned in the source. The two combine in the story the model records for the Go gob: the order of a map the source serialized changes between runs, so an encoding built on iteration order is unstable by the language's design.

**`Y1` prices bytes, this prices sequence.** `Y1` charges a build that is not byte-reproducible. `C5` charges the run-time sequence a program cannot pin. An artifact built once from pinned inputs can still print its map in three orders on three runs.

**The exemption is a specified order, not a discipline.** Insertion-order-guaranteed defaults are exempt: Python's dict (specified since 3.7), Ruby's Hash, PHP's array, Kotlin's mapOf, Dart's Map, Elixir's and Erlang's maps (key term order), Haskell's Map (key order), Crystal's Hash, Tcl's dicts, JavaScript's object key order (ES specification) and Map (insertion order). Where the unordered container is the opt-in and the ordered type is the default, the page records no charge. Where the unordered type is the default and the ordered type the opt-in, the mechanism is present, as the mitigation rule prices it.

mechanisms.label: aliasing by default
mechanisms.title: One Value, Many Names, No Declaration

criteria.text: A value is reachable through more than one name, and the declaration names no alias set. A parameter, a field, a closure, and a return can all reach the same object, and the write that matters is the one through the name the reader was not watching. The code shows the names; it does not show the sharing. In the languages where every object moves by reference, sharing is the default condition of data, not a construct a programmer reaches for.

Alias coupling: every reader of a mutated value must agree on which of its names are aliases of one storage, and the type system records the names, not the edges. The agreement is per mutation site — invisible, uncounted, and reconstructed by reading the whole reachability set — so a change at one reader must assume the writer list the declaration never stated. Where the language names the borrow, the list is in the type; where it does not, the list is folklore.

In Java every object variable is a reference, and an array's buffer is shared by assignment (a defensive copy is a discipline, not a type). In C, pointers alias freely and restrict is an opt-in promise the compiler does not check. Fortran's argument association passes the caller's storage to the callee. COBOL CALL USING passes parameter addresses. VB6 parameters are ByRef by default. Go's slices and maps share backing structures — append to a slice can write a buffer another name reads. Against these: Rust's &mut names the exclusive path; Pascal's VAR names the alias; ABAP's BY VALUE and BY REFERENCE are written in the declaration; IEC 61131-3 names REF_TO; SPARK proves flow.

**`M4` prices the owner; this prices the visible write.** `M4` charges the missing record of who frees storage — a lifetime fact, removed by a collector. `C6` charges the missing record of which names reach one value — a mutation-visibility fact, which a collector does not remove: a garbage-collected Java program needs no owner story and keeps the alias story.

**`K2` prices the thread crossing; this prices the sequential pair.** `K2` charges concurrent sharing by default. `C6` charges that a write through one name is visible through another on one thread. A language can be `K2`-clean and `C6`-charged (Clojure's immutable data with explicit refs), and the two are charged on different facts.

**`C1` prices the global; this prices the pair.** `C1` charges mutable state any module can reach. `C6` charges the local graph: names in one program unit reaching one value with no declared alias set. Both are agreements over who writes what; the scopes differ.

**The exemption is named semantics, not immutability of style.** Immutable-by-default languages (Haskell, Erlang, Elixir, Clojure's persistent data, PureScript, Gleam, Unison, Rocq, Lean) reach no mutable sharing: the harm has no site. Value-semantics languages (PHP's arrays, R and MATLAB copy-on-modify, Tcl's value copies, ABAP's named BY VALUE/BY REFERENCE, Pascal's named VAR, Rust's borrows, IEC's REF_TO, SPARK's contracts) name the alias where the alias is allowed, and the naming settles the agreement. The mitigation rule prices the default code: Java's clone, C#'s readonly, Kotlin's val, a team's copy convention — all disciplines on a shared default. Assembly carries no charge here: it makes no binding declarations for the sharing to appear in — the same 'no typed promises' boundary that exempts it from `M6`.

The programmer decides when storage is released, and the program is wrong if the decision is wrong in either direction — a missed release leaks, and a doubled release corrupts. The heap becomes a shared resource, and "who frees this, and when" is a question that every path through the program must answer identically.

Lifetime coupling: every path that holds a value must agree on when it stops being valid, because the decision is written per path rather than once for the value. The agreement is global in effect and local in expression, so one divergent path corrupts what the others still trust.

`malloc` and `free` in C. A stack frame plus `malloc` plus `free` in Assembly. `New` and `Dispose` in Turbo Pascal. Zig's `allocator.free`. In Fortran, `allocate` and `deallocate` are written by hand for a `pointer`, and a missing statement leaks.
**Presence follows the ordinary path.** A language with an optional collector for one allocation class is charged when the ordinary path is manual, because the ordinary path carries the cost.

mechanisms.label: GC non-deterministic pauses
mechanisms.title: Garbage collection on a schedule the program cannot state

criteria.text: Memory returns when the collector decides, not when the last reference goes away. The heap becomes a shared resource whose release schedule the program cannot name, so a latency-sensitive path is coupled to a component it never calls.

Schedule coupling: every path that depends on latency and the runtime must agree on when memory returns, because the release is the collector's decision and not the program's. The agreement is unavoidable and unnamed: no declaration states the schedule that the path is relying on.

The JVM family (Java, Kotlin, Scala, Groovy, Clojure), the CLR (C#, F#), Go, Crystal, D, Nim, OCaml, Haskell, Dart, Unison, and the Lisp family (Common Lisp, Racket, Scheme). Elixir, Erlang, JavaScript, and Ruby each collect on their own runtime's schedule, and TypeScript inherits the JavaScript runtime's.

**Presence does not mean "the language has a collector for one thing".** Reference counting is deterministic and is not `M2`: Swift's ARC and Delphi's strings and interfaces release at the last reference, and Delphi on Windows frees objects explicitly, so neither is charged. Objective-C is charged, because an autorelease pool defers a release past the last reference and a Core Foundation handle is released by hand.

Nothing runs automatically when a scope ends, so a resource is released in a `finally`, by a project convention, or not at all. The resource — a lock, a file, a connection — is shared, and its release depends on every path remembering.

Release coupling: every exit path must run the same release, because no scope boundary runs it for them. The agreement is duplicated on every branch, so its cost grows with the number of paths rather than with the resource.

C reaches a release path through `goto cleanup`. R uses `on.exit` and MATLAB uses `onCleanup`. Java's `try-with-resources` was added precisely to supply the destructor the language lacks. Python's `with` covers context managers, but only the ones that exist.
**Minor because one convention removes it**, and because a missed release is often caught in testing. Rust's `Drop` and Zig's `defer` run at scope exit by construction, so neither is charged.

The language does not track which of several handles owns a resource, and aliasing is unrestricted. "Who may free or mutate this?" becomes a shared resource that the program states in comments rather than in the type, and every reader has to reconstruct the answer.

Ownership coupling: every holder of a handle must agree on who may free it and who may mutate it, because the type records neither. The agreement is left to prose, so it cannot be reviewed and does not survive the author.

In C, two pointers can share one buffer with no way to say who owns it. In C++ a raw pointer and a reference alias the same object. Go offers no way to declare that a value moves, so a slice and its backing array stay aliased. In C# and Java, any two references can reach the same mutable object.
**Presence does not mean "the language has references".** Rust is not charged: moves, borrows, and lifetimes are exactly the construct whose absence `M4` records.

mechanisms.label: uninitialized reads
mechanisms.title: A Read Can Return a Value Nobody Wrote

criteria.text: Storage exists before the program fills it, and the language permits a read of the bytes nobody wrote. A local variable, a raw allocation, or an unfilled buffer arrives carrying whatever the previous user of that memory left, so the value a read returns is a property of the heap's and stack's history, which no reader of the code can see. The behavior is not a language error — it is undefined, which is the strongest way a language can decline to say.

Initialization coupling: every read must agree with a write that happened earlier on every path that reaches it, because the language keeps no record of the write. The agreement is invisible — no type, no signature, and no contract names it — so each reader reconstructs the history from the call graph, and one new path that skips the write silently reopens the question.

In C, reading an automatic object before initialization is undefined behaviour, and malloc returns bytes nobody wrote. Fortran locals without SAVE or an initializer are undefined at entry. COBOL data items without a VALUE clause hold undefined content at program start. Java gives every field a zero value and requires assignment before a local is read; C# has definite assignment; Zig zero-initializes and makes `undefined` an explicit opt-in.

**`Q1` prices the address, not the content.** `Q1` charges access outside an object's bounds and access to freed storage — both read memory the program never owned. This mechanism charges memory the program owns but has not written. The two are the classic pairing: an uninitialized length feeds an out-of-bounds write, and one violation causes the other, but each is a distinct fact and they are charged once each.

**`M1` prices the release, not the first write.** `M1` charges the decision about when storage is freed. This mechanism charges the state of the storage before the first assignment. A collector removes `M1` and leaves this one untouched: Java's collector never frees early and never leaves a read uninitialized.
**`M4` prices the owner, not the origin.** `M4` charges the missing record of who may free or mutate. This mechanism charges the missing write before the first read.

**The boundary is the written value, not the warning.** Managed runtimes that zero-initialize (the Java and .NET families, Go, Python, the dynamic languages) are not charged. Languages that initialize some types and leave others indeterminate (Delphi's managed strings against its plain records) are charged, and the page states the split. Languages that make `undefined` an explicit opt-in (Zig) are not charged, because the opt-out is named at every use site. A compiler warning is a mitigation and never an exemption.

mechanisms.label: unchecked reinterpretation
mechanisms.title: Bytes Can Be Read as a Type They Never Were

criteria.text: The language permits the same storage to be read and written through unrelated types. A union member, a pointer cast, a redefining data clause, or a reinterpret intrinsic takes the bytes of one type and hands them to another, and no check runs. The value does not satisfy the target type's constraints, and the language's own guarantee — that a value of a type is a valid value of that type — ends at the pun, unmarked, in ordinary code.

Representation coupling: every reader of the storage must agree on which type's rules govern it now, because the language records no switch. The agreement is invisible at the use site — the pun and the ordinary use of the type look identical — so each reader reconstructs which invariants still hold from the history of the bytes, and one new writer under the other type silently invalidates them all.

C unions and pointer casts; C++ `reinterpret_cast` and unchecked downcasts; COBOL REDEFINES; Fortran EQUIVALENCE and the TRANSFER intrinsic; Pascal and Delphi variant records and absolute declarations; D's cast between unrelated pointer types, which the specification hands to the programmer as undefined behaviour; Nim's cast, which the manual defines as type punning, like `reinterpret_cast`. Against these: Java and C# check every cast at run time; Rust confines it to the marked `transmute`; Go to `unsafe.Pointer`; Swift to `unsafeBitCast`; Ada names every conversion as an `Unchecked_Conversion` instantiation over one type pair.

**`Q1` prices the address, this prices the type.** `Q1` charges storage the program never owned — out of bounds, already freed. This mechanism charges storage the program owns, interpreted under rules it does not satisfy. The classic pairing runs one way into the other: pun the type, break the invariant, corrupt the memory. Each is a distinct fact and they are charged once each.

**`Q2` prices the trust boundary, this prices the program's own types.** `Q2` charges untyped data arriving from outside. This mechanism needs no untrusted input: the types lie to each other inside one program, under one programmer.

**`T7` prices the type parameter that is gone, this prices the type that is present and lied about.** `T7` charges erasure and reflection — types unreachable or alterable at run time. This mechanism charges concrete storage reinterpreted under an unrelated layout, with every type still present in the source.

**The boundary: a marked escape, a checked cast, or no invariant to break.** A checked cast prices nothing — the run time rejects the mismatch loudly (the Java and C# cast checks). A marked escape prices nothing — `transmute`, `unsafe.Pointer`, `unsafeBitCast`, and Ada's named `Unchecked_Conversion` instantiation put the crossing in the source, where review and proof can find it. Reinterpretation between plain-data types prices nothing — where every bit pattern is a valid value of the target type, no invariant can break, which is why Julia's size-checked `reinterpret` over bitstypes is not charged. And a language with no typed promises prices nothing — Assembly has no type system for the bytes to betray.

The language has no construct that carries a failure from where it is detected to where it is handled. The failure travels by side channel — a return code, an out-parameter, a log line, a global status flag — so every caller must remember to check it, and nothing checks that a caller did.

Failure-signalling coupling: producer and consumer must agree that a particular value means failure, because the language gives the failure no type. The agreement is a convention that every call site repeats, so it is invisible where it is skipped.

C returns a sentinel and sets `errno`. A shell returns an exit code that nothing reads unless `set -e` is set. Fortran reports through `iostat=`, and COBOL through `FILE STATUS`. SAS writes a note to the log and moves to the next observation. VBScript's `On Error Resume Next` turns a failure into a silent continuation.
**Presence records the path, not its enforcement.** A language whose ordinary failure path is an exception is charged `Er2` instead.

mechanisms.label: unchecked exceptions only
mechanisms.title: Failures nobody is required to handle

criteria.text: A failure can be raised without the signature saying so, and no caller is required to handle it. The set of failures a call can produce becomes a shared resource that the type system does not carry, so a caller discovers it in production.

Failure-enumeration coupling: the caller must agree with the callee on the set of failures that may arrive, because no signature lists them. The agreement is learned from production, so it is discovered after it is needed.

A MATLAB `MException` propagates until something catches it, and nothing must. An R condition is signalled and carried on. D's `throw` needs no declaration, and `nothrow` is an opt-in promise that no caller sees. Go's `panic` is unchecked and `recover` is optional. Java's unchecked exceptions carry the failures that actually occur — `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException` — even though the language also has checked ones.

**Presence does not mean "the language has no checked failures".** The criterion is charged when the failures that arrive in practice are the unchecked ones, because those are the ones no signature can enumerate.

The language lets a failure pass without any decision, and it does not force exhaustiveness. "Handled or not" becomes a shared decision that nothing records, so a caller's silence is indistinguishable from its approval.

Handling-decision coupling: each caller must agree with the rest of the system that silence is an adequate response, because nothing forces the decision to be recorded. The agreement is indistinguishable from neglect, so review cannot separate the two.

In C a return value and an `errno` value carry no consequence until the code branches on them, and a `switch` over an `enum` may leave cases unhandled without a diagnostic. In Haskell a non-exhaustive pattern compiles and fails only when reached. A `-1` from an Assembly call is a value, not a signal.

**Minor because one discipline removes it locally** — a checked return, a total `switch`, an exhaustive match — but the discipline has to be written down, and the language will not check that it is kept.

A failure cannot be carried as an ordinary value through an ordinary expression, so it cannot be threaded, combined, or returned from a helper. The success-and-failure pair has to be rebuilt at every level, through out-parameters, sentinel values, or a global status, so the *shape* of the error path becomes a shared convention.

Error-shape coupling: every level must agree on where a failure travels, because no value can carry it through an expression. The agreement is repeated at each boundary, so a change to the shape changes every signature in the chain.

Ada reports through `raise`, so a fallible operation cannot be folded into an expression. In C the pair is an out-parameter or `errno`. In Go it is a second return value, which cannot be mapped or chained without a second statement. In Assembly there is no value that can carry "this failed".

**Minor because the cost is syntactic rather than structural** — but it is the difference between an error path that composes and one that is everywhere a special case. Rust's `Result`, Haskell's `Either`, and C++'s `std::expected` are the constructs whose absence is charged.

mechanisms.label: no isolation unit for a fault
mechanisms.title: One Fault Ends the Program

criteria.text: A fault has no declared survivable unit. The language raises and catches inside one frame chain; the runtime publishes no supervision unit whose failure the program survives. An uncaught fault in a thread takes the process with it (the .NET and C++ and OCaml documentation says so in plain terms), a Go panic unwinds every goroutine, a Swift trap aborts, a PLC task crash is the runtime's problem, an ABEND ends the program. The maintainer has no named recoverable boundary: the choices are a process restart set up by the deployment, or a catch in a frame that is already unwound.

Fault-boundary coupling: the agreement between a unit of work and its survivability is held nowhere in the program. Recovery discipline — wrap the worker loop, restart the service, keep the shared state recoverable — is an untyped convention across the codebase, and every failure mode the convention missed is a full restart. Where the runtime publishes a supervision unit the program declares, the agreement moves into a declared structure, and the charge lifts.

The .NET runtime documents that an unhandled exception terminates the process. C++ documents std::terminate for a thread with an uncaught exception. The Go specification: an unrecovered panic terminates the program. Swift traps abort. OCaml, Nim, Crystal, and D document the thread-wide end. Fortran STOPs; COBOL abends. Against these: the BEAM publishes the supervision tree — a process fault restarts the process under a declared strategy; the JVM documents thread death as the end of the thread; Python's threading documentation ends the thread, not the process; Ada's RM 11.1 terminates the task that raises and the partition survives; Common Lisp's restarts are first-class recovery points; JavaScript publishes Workers.

**`Er1` prices the missing structured path; this prices the missing boundary.** `Er1` charges a language with no structured failure mechanism at all. A language can ship exceptions (Er1 absent) and publish no survivable unit — C++, PHP, the .NET family — and a language can ship a unit with a blunt path. The two facts are separate: raising and surviving are different agreements.

**`K4` prices the concurrency scope; this prices fault containment.** `K4` charges the lack of structured concurrent scoping. `Er5` charges that a fault in a unit of work is not contained by a unit the runtime publishes. BEAM languages carry both answers (supervision is the published unit); a thread-isolated runtime (JVM, Python) answers containment without publishing supervision; a process-abort runtime (Go, Swift, .NET) carries the charge.

**Runtime, not language.** The tag says the executor decides: which unit survives a fault is the runtime's published contract, not the source text. The published exemptions the model honors: BEAM supervision trees (Erlang, Elixir, Gleam), JVM thread death (Java family), Python's threading contract, Ada task termination (RM 11.1), Julia's failed tasks, Common Lisp's restarts, JavaScript Workers, Lua coroutines, Tcl interpreters, SQL transactions, EVM transactions, PLC tasks, R's session, SAS's step, ABAP's internal session, Scratch's script, FoxPro's ON ERROR, VB6's On Error, Prolog's queries (an uncaught exception fails the query and the toplevel continues, documented in the standard systems), and GML's script termination (a script error ends the script, documented in the manual). The declaration-shaped exemption is the program naming the unit; a convention is not a unit.

The ordinary execution model offers no second thread of control: running two computations at once needs a worker, a separate process, or a native extension. "How much may run at once" is fixed by the runtime, so every part of the program that wants throughput is coupled to that one decision.

Throughput coupling: every part of a design that needs concurrency must agree with the runtime on how a second thread may exist, because the execution model is fixed outside the language. The agreement cannot be made locally: a second core is available only by leaving the program's own structure behind.

Python's global interpreter lock serialises bytecode execution, so a CPU-bound program must leave the language — multiprocessing, a native extension — to use a second core. JavaScript and PHP take a request or an event as the unit of work. Solidity runs a transaction on one EVM thread, and PureScript and TypeScript inherit the single-threaded JavaScript runtime.

**Presence is about what the language can express**, not about what a library can reach. A language whose only route to a second core is a separate process or a native extension is charged, because the program's structure is then not the language's.
Concurrency shares memory by default, and nothing marks a value as thread-local, immutable, or owned. The shared cell becomes the resource, and every reader has to reconstruct which lock protects it.

Shared-cell coupling: every thread that reaches a value must agree on its content, because the default offers no privacy and no immutability. The agreement is unbounded — a thread's correctness depends on code it does not contain.

An Assembly store to a global is visible to every core, with no privacy notion attached to the address. A PL/SQL package variable is shared by every program unit in the session. In T-SQL, `SET` options and session-scoped state are visible to code the caller did not write. A C file-scope object is shared by every thread that reaches it.

**Presence records the *default*.** `K2` and `K3` often appear together, and they are different claims: `K2` says the shared state is the default, and `K3` says the language gives no help in finding the resulting races.

Locks and atomics are library types, and the language neither proves the locking discipline nor detects a race. The discipline becomes an agreement across every file that touches the data, and the compiler checks none of it.

Protocol coupling: every file that touches the data must agree on one locking discipline, because the language supplies primitives but no proof. The agreement is horizontal — it runs across files that never call each other — so no compiler can hold it and no test can localise a violation.

Java's `synchronized`, C#'s `lock`, Go's `sync.Mutex`, Kotlin's `@Synchronized`, and Scala's synchronized blocks serialise access but do not find a missing lock. D's `core.atomic` and Crystal's `Mutex` and `WaitGroup` are libraries over the same primitive. A `lock` prefix on one x86-64 instruction is the whole of Assembly's provision.
**Presence is about detection, not about threads.** A language that proves thread safety at compile time is not charged, even though it has threads.

The language gives no construct that scopes a task's lifetime to a block, so nothing guarantees that a task has finished when the block ends. The task's lifetime becomes a shared resource that the program tracks by hand, and a scope can end while work it started is still running.

Task-lifetime coupling: the block that starts work must agree with the work about when it ends, because nothing scopes the two together. The agreement is kept by hand, so every starter must also be the joiner.

C's threads and Zig's threads have no scope that joins them. Perl's `threads` leaves the task tree to the program. A Groovy executor service is joined by hand or not at all. In Assembly a thread is a `clone` or `pthread_create` call with nothing around it.

**Minor because a scope construct can be added by convention**, and because the failure it causes — work outliving its scope — is usually visible in testing. Kotlin's `coroutineScope` and Swift's task groups are the constructs whose absence is charged.

The language has no first-class lock, channel, or await, so concurrent work is started and steered outside the language. The synchronisation becomes a shared resource that lives in signals, exit codes, or a foreign library, so no declaration states the protocol.

Coordination coupling: the concurrent units must agree on a protocol, because the language supplies no first-class lock, channel, or await to state it. The agreement is carried by the operating system's facilities rather than by the program's declarations.

A shell starts a job with `&`, steers it with signals, and communicates through exit codes, with no lock and no channel anywhere in the language. Turbo Pascal 7.0 in DOS reaches concurrent work through an interrupt procedure, and its synchronisation is the hardware's.
**Presence is the complement of `K1`.** `K1` is a runtime that forbids parallelism; `K5` is a language that offers nothing to coordinate it.

A concurrent task is an operating-system thread, so each task holds a thread for its whole lifetime. The number of tasks a program may run at once becomes a platform limit, and a task that blocks holds a thread that another task could have used.
Scale coupling: the program's concurrency structure is fixed by the runtime's mapping from task to thread, so a design that reads well at ten tasks is a liability at ten thousand.

Java before virtual threads gives each request a platform thread, so a blocking call consumes one. Kotlin's coroutines, Swift's tasks, Go's goroutines, Erlang's processes, and Haskell's green threads multiplex many tasks onto a few threads, so none is charged. Java 21's virtual threads remove the charge for Java 21 and later.

**Presence asks whether the ordinary unit is an OS thread.** A single-threaded event loop is not charged, because no task holds a thread. An implementation that multiplexes tasks onto threads — green threads, coroutines, goroutines, processes — is not charged either, because the mapping is the runtime's and it is cheap.

mechanisms.label: cannot function outside one vendor/domain
mechanisms.title: Cannot leave one vendor or one domain

criteria.text: The program runs only inside one vendor's product or one domain, so the deployment unit *is* that platform. The platform is the widest shared resource of all: every line is coupled to a runtime, an API surface, and a release cycle the program does not control.

Platform coupling: the whole program must agree with an environment it cannot change, because the deployment unit and the artifact are the same thing. Nothing in the source stands outside the agreement, which is what makes the tier High.

A PL/SQL program needs an Oracle-family database and deploys as a schema. SAS needs a SAS installation and deploys as a library on a SAS host. Transact-SQL needs SQL Server, Azure SQL, or SAP ASE. A Rocq development runs only after extraction to another language. An x86-64 Assembly artifact runs only where that instruction set runs. A Solidity contract runs only on an EVM.
**Presence is about the artifact.** A language whose compiler runs anywhere but whose programs run in one place is still charged.

mechanisms.label: single-vendor but other uses
mechanisms.title: One vendor dominates, other uses exist

criteria.text: The language has a single dominant implementation or platform, even though alternatives exist in principle. The toolchain, the library set, and the release schedule of one vendor become the program's agreed reality.

Implementation coupling: a single implementation's compiler, libraries, and release cycle become the agreement every consumer makes, because the alternatives are theoretical rather than practical. The escape exists on paper, and the working reality is one vendor's.

Groovy has no non-JVM implementation. Objective-C's complete language, reference compiler, and flagship frameworks are one vendor's. Most production COBOL runs on one mainframe platform with that vendor's compilers. Eiffel's practical toolchain is EiffelStudio, and Tcl's is its own interpreter. Swift's toolchain and frameworks are one platform's.
**P2 is a degree below `P1`.** The artifact could in principle run elsewhere, and in practice does not.

The program targets a platform that is no longer developed, so the artifact is frozen with it. The platform's limits — its word size, its memory model, its APIs — become permanent constraints on the program.
Era coupling: the program must agree with a platform whose own development has ended, because the artifact is frozen at that platform's last state. The agreement has no revision path, only an exit.
Turbo Pascal 7.0 compiles real-mode DOS executables, and it was the last release of that line: the target, not just the tool, has ended.

**`P3` is not `P1`.** `P1` is one live vendor with one domain; `P3` is a platform whose own life has ended. Assembly on x86-64 is charged `P1` for its instruction-set lock-in, and not `P3`, because that instruction set is current.

The language is a bad fit for ordinary application work, because the constructs it lacks make ordinary logic expensive. Every abstraction the program needs has to be built from primitives, so the program's structure becomes a local invention rather than a shared convention.

Expressiveness coupling: every ordinary abstraction must agree with the primitives the language supplies, because nothing above them is standard. The agreement is made per project, so two programs in the language share a language and little else.

Assembly has no types, no data abstraction, and no error path, so application logic is expensive to write and to change. Scratch has no file access, no network, and no general library, so it is not usable for a production application. Prolog's computation model fits relational search and resists ordinary imperative application code. Ada's and Fortran's constructs fit their own problem classes first.

**Presence is judged against general-purpose use**, not against the language's intended domain — otherwise every domain-specific language would be charged twice, once for its fit and once for its narrowness.

The source is executed by an interpreter or a virtual machine rather than compiled to the machine's code ahead of time. The execution model becomes a shared resource fixed by the runtime, so the shape of every hot loop is decided by the interpreter's dispatch rather than by the algorithm.

Execution-model coupling: the shape of every hot path must agree with the interpreter's dispatch rather than with the algorithm, because the runtime decides how a statement is executed. The agreement is invisible in the source, so a hot loop is tuned by leaving the language rather than by rewriting it.

A Prolog goal is a search over the clause database through the engine's instruction set, so a tight arithmetic loop trails a compiled equivalent. A shell parses and evaluates text at run time, so a loop over files pays parser cost per iteration. Base R and base MATLAB execute an interpreted form, and Perl's reference interpreter has no JIT. Ruby is charged because its JIT is opt-in, so a default run stays interpreted.

**Presence does not mean "slow".** The criterion is about the *absence of an ahead-of-time path*, which is why a language with a mature library behind it (MATLAB's BLAS and LAPACK calls) can still be charged while remaining fast where it matters.

mechanisms.label: GC pauses
mechanisms.title: Collector pauses visible to the program

criteria.text: A collector's pause is part of the program's timing, and the program cannot state when it will occur. The heap's release schedule becomes a shared resource decided outside the program, so a latency target couples to the runtime's collector.

Timing coupling: a latency budget must agree with the collector's pause, because the program cannot schedule the pause. The agreement is temporal rather than structural — it constrains when the program runs, not what it contains.

Dart's generational collector stops the mutator, which shows as a frame-time spike. SBCL and CCL stop the program to collect Common Lisp, GHC pauses to collect Haskell, and Nim's collector stalls its mutator. The JVM's pause reaches Java, Kotlin, Scala, and Groovy alike, and the CLR's reaches C#, F#, and the Visual Basic runtime. JavaScript pauses the one event loop it has, so a pause blocks every pending callback, and TypeScript and PureScript inherit that runtime. Go's pause is short but present, Eiffel's and D's collectors remain a latency risk, and Unison's own runtime collects on its own schedule.

**`R2` is not `M2`.** `M2` records that the heap's schedule is not the program's; `R2` records that the schedule is *observable* — a pause a latency budget has to absorb. The two are marked independently: a language can hold `M2` without `R2`, because a collector whose pause the page does not record as a cost (Python's, Ruby's, Crystal's, Racket's) is not charged. Where the page records the pause as a cost, the mechanism is charged — which is what keeps the charge set checkable against the pages themselves.

The first execution of a function compiles it, so the code's speed depends on which path runs first and on how long the process has been up. Measurement itself becomes the shared convention: a benchmark has to agree on a warm-up, and a short-lived process never reaches the optimized state.

Measurement coupling: a benchmark, a latency target, and the compiler must agree on what "steady state" means, because the first execution compiles the code. The agreement must be written down, so a short-lived process and a long-lived one are not measuring the same program.

Julia compiles a method on its first call, so latency depends on which path runs first. The JVM and the CLR tier their compilation, so Groovy, Clojure, Kotlin, F#, C#, Java, and PowerShell are slower on their first requests than in steady state.
**Minor because a long-running process amortises it**, and because it can be pre-warmed.

The language has no standard way to declare, fetch, and resolve a dependency. The build's dependency graph becomes a shared resource owned by the build system rather than the language, so a project's dependencies are a local convention that no tool can check.

Dependency-graph coupling: a project's dependencies must agree with a build script rather than with a resolver, because the language defines no way to declare them. The agreement is local and unchecked, so two checkouts can disagree about the graph.

In Assembly a dependency is an object file or a linked library resolved by the build script. The C and C++ standard defines no distribution, so the platform's toolchain supplies one. Prolog's standard defines no distribution, so each system ships its own. A shell has no dependency declaration beyond what the script itself probes for.
**Minor because the cost is confined to the build** — but the build's convention is the whole program's convention.

No single toolchain covers the language, so every tool targets a dialect, a version, or a vendor. The workflow becomes a shared resource with several incompatible owners, and a team's tooling choices must agree file by file.

Toolchain coupling: a project's tools must agree with a dialect or a version rather than with the language, because no single toolchain covers the whole of it. The agreement is assembled per tool, so each choice constrains the next one.

ORMs, migration tools, linters, and formatters each target one SQL engine's dialect, so there is no single SQL toolchain. C and C++ are split across platform toolchains with different extensions and different warning sets. Go's module and build conventions grew in parallel with the wider Go toolchain, so a project's conventions are partly its own.
**Moderate because the fragmentation is structural** — it comes from the language's reach, not from anyone's neglect.

The library pool, the hiring market, or the vendor's investment is small, so more code is written than found. The library surface is a shared resource the whole community draws on, and when it is thin, each project re-invents and the local convention becomes the only one.

Supply coupling: the program must agree to write what the community does not supply, because the library pool is thin. The agreement is with a market as much as with a language — hiring, support, and examples move with it.

`dub`'s registry is far smaller than crates.io, npm, or Maven, so a D project is likelier to write a library than to find one. SAS's market shrank against R and Python, so new packages arrive more slowly. Tcl, Eiffel, Prolog, Delphi, Crystal, and Lua sit in the same position. This criterion is charged in just over half the inventory, and it is deliberately held at Moderate: a niche language is a cost, not a defect.

The engine, the tooling, and the documentation come from one vendor under licence. The right to continue becomes a shared resource owned by a licensor, so the program's future depends on a commercial decision.

Licence coupling: the program must agree with a commercial owner's terms, because the engine, the tools, and the documentation come under one licence. The agreement reaches past the code into procurement and support.

MATLAB's toolboxes, editor, and reference documentation come from one vendor under licence. PL/SQL's engine, tooling, and support come from Oracle. SAS, COBOL, Eiffel, Transact-SQL, Objective-C, and VBScript are in the same position, and so is any language whose manuals are behind a paywall.
**Moderate because the licence is a structural dependency**, not merely a price: the artifacts, the formats, and the support channel are all the vendor's.

The build, the debugger, or the package tooling runs on one operating system or one runtime only. The development environment becomes a shared resource the team cannot choose, so the workflow is coupled to a platform.

Environment coupling: the team's build, debugger, and package tools must agree with one operating system, because the toolchain is written for it alone. The agreement constrains the team rather than the program — the artifact may still be portable.
Swift's toolchain, its debugger, and its frameworks belong to one platform, so a Swift team outside it works with a second-class toolchain.
**Ec5 is not `P2`.** `P2` is about where the *program* runs; `Ec5` is about where the *tools* run.

One framework, library, or runtime dominates to the point that the alternatives are not really alternatives. The dominant choice becomes a shared resource with one owner, so the whole community's assumptions move together — and a defect or a policy change in that one component reaches everything.

Concentration coupling: the community's assumptions must agree with one dominant component, because the alternatives are not maintained enough to be escapes. The agreement delivers consistency and removes the exit at the same time.

Elixir's ecosystem is a monoculture around Phoenix and OTP, so alternatives to the dominant framework are few. Java's and C#'s enterprise worlds, PHP's web stack, and Ruby's Rails are each dominated by one framework family.
**Moderate because the concentration is a risk, not a defect**: it delivers consistency, and it removes the escape route.

The ecosystem carries versions, APIs, or idioms that must still be supported, so old and new coexist. The compatibility surface becomes a shared resource that every new feature has to respect, so no part of the ecosystem can change freely.

Compatibility coupling: every new feature must agree with every version still in service, because the ecosystem will not drop them. The agreement is longitudinal — it runs between old and new code rather than between modules.

Java's enterprise stack keeps a 1999-era API in service next to a 2026 one, and a library has to keep both working. Ruby's ecosystem pins older runtimes through older gems, so an upgrade has to wait for the slowest dependency.
**`Ec7` is the twin of `V1`.** `V1` is the language changing under the code; `Ec7` is the ecosystem refusing to change.

mechanisms.label: unpromised binary boundary
mechanisms.title: Compiled Units Cross a Release Unpromised

criteria.text: A compiled unit of the language reaches a consumer who links it without rebuilding it, and no published promise says that the producer's release and the consumer's release agree. The agreement is the toolchain release. Nothing in the source of either side names it. Where a check exists, it fires at load or at link, after both sides are already built. The failure names a mismatch, and the consumer still works out which side to rebuild.

Release-boundary coupling at a published binary: a wheel, a plugin, a MEX file, an extension, a package, a library, or a model package names the release that built it, and every consumer who cannot rebuild carries the whole cost. The agreement runs between independently released parts, so one release in one part forces rebuilds in all the others. A source-shipped package resolves the same agreement inside the consumer's own build, and a published promise settles it: the class-file rules a language specification publishes, the assembly format and compatibility rules a runtime publishes. Neither is charged.

A Python wheel names the interpreter, ABI, and platform tags, and the installer loads that binary. A Go plugin must be built with the same toolchain as the application that opens it. MathWorks requires a MEX file to be rebuilt for a new release. libstdc++ documents that binaries built with one GNU release are incompatible with binaries built with another.

**Delivery targets decide this mechanism, target by target.** Every language page lists its delivery targets at the end of its Ecosystem coupling section: what ships, whether a compiled unit reaches a consumer who does not rebuild it, and whether a published promise covers it. The mechanism is present exactly when one target crosses with no promise. Kotlin is charged on `.klib` and not on the JVM jar. JavaScript is charged on a node-gyp addon and not on a Node-API addon. Go is charged on its plugin path and not on its module proxy. Rust, Dart, Julia, Swift, and Zig are not charged: their package managers ship source, and the compiled paths they publish carry a promise. C and the Java family are not charged on objects that travel on a published format.

**A promise must be published, and a charge needs a document.** A de-facto convention settles nothing: an ecosystem that mostly works across releases is not exempted by practice, and an ecosystem with no document at all is not charged on practice either. Each charged verdict names the document it rests on, and each exemption names the guarantee it claims; no verdict is priced from practice alone. Where a vendor document is out of print and no current document decides, the page records the fact in the delivery table and the score stays untouched.

**`T14` prices a different agreement.** `T14` charges the hand-written declaration a developer maintains at a foreign-language boundary. This mechanism charges the release boundary of a unit that crosses as a binary. A plugin host and a foreign binding are two facts, and they are charged once each.

mechanisms.label: unpromised data boundary
mechanisms.title: Stored State Crosses a Release Unpromised

criteria.text: State the program writes outlives the program: a serialized value, a workspace image, a compiled snapshot, a project archive, a saved model. The file carries a format header naming the release that wrote it, and the only reader is the toolchain. The boundary crosses time in one direction the consumer cannot rebuild: the data is years old, the release is today's. Where a version check exists, it fires when the file opens. Where the vendor withdraws a reader, files written years ago have no reader at all on the current release, and the failure is not a link error to fix — it is the data.

Release-boundary coupling at stored state: the agreement runs across time, between the release that wrote the file and the release reading it now. The upgrade of a toolchain is safe for old data only when the vendor has promised it, and a promise is published in one direction. A format with a version field and a published reading rule settles the agreement — the reader checks the header and reads; the file is not charged. A format that records its writer in the header, states no rule, and leaves the maintainer to discover the reading by opening the file keeps the agreement unpromised, and that is what the mechanism charges.

Microsoft disables BinaryFormatter in .NET 8 and removes the in-box implementation in .NET 9, so payloads written on an older runtime have no reader on the current one. R states that serialization format 3, the default for save() and saveRDS() since 3.6.0, cannot be read by versions of R prior to 3.5.0. Python reserves the right to change the marshal format, which .pyc files carry, in non-backwards compatible ways. MATLAB states that releases R2006b and later all support all MAT file versions, and Java's serialization specification publishes the stream protocol, its versions, and the serial version UID.

**Data-format targets decide this mechanism, target by target.** Every language page that stores state lists its data formats at the end of its Ecosystem coupling section, under the delivery table: what the toolchain stores, whether the current release reads data written by an older one as a published promise, and whether the vendor states that data written now cannot be read by other releases. The mechanism is present exactly when one row carries a break: the reading promise published as broken, the writing direction published as unreadable elsewhere, or a break the probe harness has reproduced with pinned releases and a committed result. Python is charged on the marshal format its .pyc files carry and is not charged on pickle, which carries the published promise. The C# family is charged on BinaryFormatter payloads, which .NET 8 disabled and .NET 9 removed. R is charged on the format-3 default it states old readers cannot open. Ruby, Perl, Go, Java, Julia, MATLAB, Scratch, Erlang, Elixir, GameMaker, and SAS carry a published promise on the format they store and are not charged. PHP is recorded, not priced: the manual names the format, documents no version field, and states no cross-release rule, and the probe harness has reproduced no break across the tested release pairs — tested is not promised, so the row records and prices nothing.

**A promise must be published, and a charge needs an affirmative fact.** The discipline is the one the delivery table applies to compiled units: practice settles nothing. A charge rests on a published statement of a break, or on a break the probe harness has reproduced — never on a suspicion of one. An ecosystem whose old files mostly open is not exempted by habit, and a format with no document is not charged on suspicion either. Each charged row names the document stating the break, or the probe artifact that reproduced it; each exemption names the document publishing the promise; and a row nothing decides is recorded and removes no points.

**`Ec8` prices a different crossing.** `Ec8` charges a compiled unit that crosses from a producer to a consumer who links it without rebuilding it. This mechanism charges state that crosses from a release to the future: the consumer is not a second team, it is the same program on a later toolchain, and it cannot rebuild the file. A wheel is `Ec8`; the pickled cache the wheel's program reads on first run is this mechanism. The two never charge one byte.

**`Ec7` prices a different burden.** `Ec7` charges the ecosystem that keeps old versions, APIs, and idioms in service, so new work must respect them. This mechanism charges the file that keeps the old release's reader required. Long-lived stored data is one reason the legacy burden lands at all; the two price the staying and the crossing, and never the same byte.
**`V1` prices a language moving under the code.** This mechanism prices a reader that no longer opens the data. The code changes under `V1`; the file's reader changes under `Ec9`.
The language, or its standard library, changes in a way that invalidates existing code. The language itself becomes the shared resource, so every consumer has to revisit code when the language moves.

Version coupling: the source must agree with one version of the language, because a later version may change the meaning it had. The agreement is temporal — the same file means different things to two compilers.

Rust's edition 2024 rewrote the capture rules of `impl Trait`, required `unsafe extern`, and reserved `gen`, so a crate that adopts the edition has to be revisited. Scala's 2-to-3 migration, Nim's and Zig's moving standard libraries, and Haskell's library-level breakage put the same cost on their users.
**An edition system is the mitigation, not the absence.** Rust isolates the changes to an opt-in edition and is still charged, because the cost of the migration is real.

The language is complete and will not change further. "What the language will do next" becomes settled, which removes one shared uncertainty — and also means that a missing feature or a defect is permanent.

Definition coupling: the program must agree with a definition that will not move again, because the language is complete. The agreement is settled rather than absent, which is why a freeze can be a benefit and a trap at once.
Objective-C 2.0 is effectively the last revision of the language, and platform-facing work moved to a successor. Turbo Pascal's definition is frozen at 7.0.
**Minor because a freeze is a promise.** Nothing in the existing code will break.

The language has no vendor, no steward, and no expectation of another version. The language becomes a shared resource that will never be maintained again, so every defect and every security issue is permanent, and every dependency is a dead end.

Stewardship coupling: the program must agree with a language that no one maintains, because there is no second party left to renegotiate with. Every defect becomes a term of the agreement, and no local escape exists because a migration path would have to be supplied by the missing steward.

Borland ended the Turbo Pascal line in the mid-1990s and moved it to a successor product. Microsoft announced VBScript's deprecation in 2023, with removal from the operating system planned after 2027, so the remaining life of the language is a published countdown.
**High because the cost is total and irreversible.** There is no migration path inside the language, and none can be added.

The language is defined by a standard that revises on a multi-year cycle, so a needed feature waits for the committee. The definition becomes a shared resource whose revision schedule is not the user's, and a program's design is bounded by when the standard catches up.

Revision coupling: the program's design must agree with a committee's calendar, because the definition moves on a multi-year cycle. The agreement is with a date rather than with a decision, so no local act can advance it.

SQL:2023 appeared seven years after SQL:2016, so a feature outside the standard stays an extension in the meantime. Ada 2022 followed Ada 2012 by a decade, and the POSIX shell specification moves slowly enough that a shell's own extensions are the practical definition of its behaviour.
**Minor because implementations commonly lead the standard** with extensions — at the cost of portability, which is charged elsewhere, under `P2` and `Ec2`.

A default that the source does not name changes between releases of the runtime or the standard library, and nothing in the build reports it. The default is the shared resource: the code and the platform must agree on a value the code never wrote down, and the platform may choose it again in the next release. No compiler error, no signature change, and no type carries the old value, so the agreement is discovered when the behaviour of the running program moves.

Default coupling: a deployment must agree with a default it does not name, and the agreement is one-sided — the platform sets it, the code inherits it, and the next release may set it again. The agreement is silent in both directions: the code records neither the value it relies on nor the fact that it relies on one.

Java 27 changed two such defaults. ML-KEM and ML-DSA private keys now encode as a `seed` rather than an expanded key, so a key this JDK writes is unreadable by an older release unless `jdk.mlkem.pkcs8.encoding` is set before the key is made. G1 replaced the Serial selection on small machines, so a deployment that never named a collector now runs a different one.
