Both are documented in the release notes and both can be reversed — by a security property or by `-XX:+UseSerialGC` — and both still move the behaviour of code that no one edited.

**This mechanism is recorded, not priced.** A price has a fixed direction: the same presence must always mean the same cost, or the sum stops being an arithmetic and becomes an opinion. The direction of a default change is not fixed. G1 everywhere helps a one-CPU container by the JEP's own measurements and moves the latency profile of a service that was measured under Serial; the `seed` encoding is better interoperability by RFC 9935 and a break for a peer on an older release. The same presence can therefore mean a gain or a loss, and a mechanism whose sign varies cannot enter a sum without making that sum incomparable across languages and across releases. Pricing it would also make the inventory anti-evolution by construction: a release that improves every default and changes no construct could only lose points. The model records the event here, states its direction in the observation beside the mark, and leaves the score to the mechanisms whose sign is fixed.

**Presence is per assessed release.** An empty mark records that no such change appears in this analysis for the release shown — not that none exists. The analysis date and the assessed version are stated on every page.

mechanisms.label: build-variant state space
mechanisms.title: The Shipped Binary Is a Configuration Nobody Tested

criteria.text: The toolchain ships a documented source-level facility that selects which source reaches the compiled artifact: a preprocessor's #ifdef tree, a build constraint, a reader conditional, a compile-time when, a code-generating %IF. The flag set is a shared resource that every guarded part of the program must agree with, and no source fully names it. A program is no longer one program: it is a space of selections, and the binary a maintainer ships is one selection. The states nobody builds are nobody's problem until a change touches a guard — then the agreement has to be reconstructed for every combination, and tested for the one that ships.

Compile-time-configuration coupling: each guard is an agreement between the source and a flag set that lives in project files, command lines, and toolchain defaults, not in the source the reader sees. The agreement multiplies: n independent flags name 2^n programs, and the suite runs one of them. A change to shared code must respect every selection that ships, and the untested selections compile wrong in silence — the failure is a build that no one ran, not a test that no one passed.

The C preprocessor and its #ifdef tree; Go's //go:build constraints; Rust's cfg; Common Lisp's #+/#- reader conditionals; Racket's read-conditional barbs; Clojure's reader conditionals; Delphi's {$IFDEF}; Erlang's -ifdef; Oracle PL/SQL's $IF/$THEN; SAS's macro %IF; X++'s #if; GHC's -XCPP; Nim's when defined; Zig's build options feeding inline-if — the release build the consumer runs compiles a program the debug suite never saw.

**`V1` prices the language moving; this prices the flags multiplying.** `V1` charges a release changing under the code, so consumers revisit source when the language moves. This mechanism charges one release's source meaning different programs under different flags. Both agreements run along time; the first is against a release, this one against a configuration.

**`G1` prices the missing tooling; this prices the space the tooling faces.** `G1` charges the absence of a test framework, assertion, or runner. This mechanism charges the number of programs a suite must face. A strong suite against ten flag states still pays ten states; a weak suite pays them worse, and the two charges are separate facts.

**The charge is the state space, not the facility's usefulness.** Conditional compilation exists to solve portability problems, and the model prices no feature. What it prices is the agreement the facility forces: every guarded file must agree with every combination that ships, the flag set lives outside the source, and the untested selections fail as silent builds. A language with no source-level selection pays none of this — Java, Kotlin, Python, Ruby, PHP, JavaScript, and the rest of the family carry no such facility, and the absence earns the absence of the mechanism, nothing more.

**Context, not language: the toolchain ships it.** A preprocessor, a build constraint, a reader conditional, a compile-time evaluation hook — the facility is a toolchain fact, decided by the vendor, so the tag is context: the remedy is outside both code and language, in what the toolchain chooses to ship. Each charged page names the facility in the observation beside the mark.

The language exists to serve one domain or one vendor's product, so adopting it is also adopting that target. The domain's model becomes the shared resource, and every abstraction in the program has to be expressible in it.

Domain-model coupling: every abstraction must agree with one target's model, because adopting the language is adopting the target. The agreement reaches the design and not only the deployment, so a choice of language settles what the program can say.

MATLAB's library set targets one vendor's platform, so adoption is a procurement decision as much as a technical one. PL/SQL exists to run inside an Oracle database, so the Oracle data tier is the only domain. SAS's data-step model is the SAS library. Transact-SQL's domain is one database engine, and Solidity's is one blockchain's execution model. Rocq's, SPARK's, and Lean's domain is machine-checked proof.

**`D1` and `P1` ask different questions.** `P1` is where the artifact can *run*; `D1` is what the language is *for*. MATLAB is charged `D1` and not `P1`: the vendor's platform is the language's purpose, and the artifact is not confined to one machine.

The idiomatic way to use the language is inside a host framework whose execution model decides the program's structure. The framework's callbacks, lifecycles, and conventions become the shared resource, so the program's architecture is set by a third party.

Architecture coupling: the program's structure must agree with a host framework's lifecycle, callbacks, and conventions, because the idiomatic path into the language runs through the framework. The agreement sits above the code — changing it means changing what calls the code, not what the code does.

A Java program is idiomatically assembled as a Spring application, so its wiring, its transactions, and its entry points follow the framework's model. A C# program follows the same path through ASP.NET. In Groovy the build script and the pipeline run inside a host's execution model and obey its conventions. Go's project layout and module conventions are conventions the toolchain assumes.
**Moderate because the framework is hard to leave**: the code is written against the framework's lifecycle, not merely called by it.

A practitioner has to learn concepts that build on nothing else they already know. That knowledge becomes a shared resource with a narrow entry, so the onboarding cost is borne by every team and every hiring decision.

Onboarding coupling: productivity must agree with a body of concepts that the practitioner's background does not supply, because the language builds on nothing familiar. The agreement is with people rather than with code, so it is paid again at every hire.

Erlang asks for functional programming, the actor model, and OTP at once, on top of a Prolog-derived syntax. Rust asks for ownership, borrows, and lifetimes. Haskell asks for type classes, monads, and laziness. Lean and Rocq ask for dependent types and proof engineering. Ada's language and its annexes are large enough that a team learns them for a while.
**`L1` measures distance from the mainstream**, so a language whose concepts are unusual is charged even when the concepts are excellent. The cost is real even when the design is good.

mechanisms.label: large surface/multi-paradigm
mechanisms.title: Large surface, or several paradigms at once

criteria.text: The language is large, or it supports several paradigms at once, so there are many ways to write the same thing. "The way we do it here" becomes the shared resource, and it has to be written down, because the language will not narrow the choice.

Idiom coupling: each contributor must agree with the team on which of several available ways to write the same thing, because the language refuses to narrow the choice. The agreement is a document rather than a check — the language will not enforce it.

Ada's standard library, annexes, and profiles add to a large core. C++ mixes four paradigms and several generations of idiom. Scala, Kotlin, F#, Elixir, Erlang, Nim, and Swift each admit both object and functional styles. PowerShell mixes cmdlets, .NET calls, and pipelines.
**Minor because a team can cut the surface** with a style guide — but the guide is the team's, not the language's.

The reference material is thin, or it omits the knowledge a practitioner actually needs. The understanding of the language becomes a shared resource held privately, so it is rediscovered by each practitioner in turn.
Knowledge coupling: understanding must agree with whoever already holds it, because the reference does not supply it. The agreement is private, so it leaves when the practitioner leaves.

In Lean 4, why a `simp` call succeeded, or why an instance was not found, has to be read out of the goal state and the option list rather than from a reference. Zig's language reference is still evolving with the language, so the authoritative answer is sometimes the compiler's source.
**Minor because it is the cheapest criterion to fix externally**: a book, a wiki, or a community can supply what the vendor did not.
The notation requires many words or lines to express a small idea. The reading surface grows, so a lower signal-to-noise ratio is a cost every reader pays on every review.

Reading-surface coupling: every reader must pay the same notation cost for the same idea, because the language requires the words. The agreement is uniform and unavoidable, which is why a local style cannot reduce it.

A PL/SQL unit needs a declaration section, a `BEGIN ... END` block, and an exception section before it does anything. A SAS step is a list of `KEYWORD option;` lines, and `LENGTH`, `FORMAT`, and `LABEL` add lines before any data is touched. COBOL and Ada require a declaration before nearly every statement, and Fortran and Delphi carry a long legacy of required keywords.
**`S1` is not a style preference.** It is charged where the language *requires* the words, not where a programmer chose them.
Comparable things are written differently, so there is no rule to learn, only cases. The syntax becomes a shared resource whose mapping is not predictable, so every reader has to look things up.

Mapping coupling: the reader must agree with a name's behaviour through memorised cases rather than through a rule, because the language supplies no predictable mapping. The agreement is per name, so it grows with the library and never generalises.

PHP's standard library names follow no single rule: `str_replace`, `strpos`, and `str_contains` disagree on placement of the underscore and on argument order between neighbours. Perl's built-ins read the current context, so `$_`, `@_`, and `%+` change what a call does.
**S2 is the most expensive syntax criterion because it cannot be automated away.** A formatter normalises layout, not names.

The notation leans on dense delimiters, so the structure is carried by characters the reader has to match. Reading then requires tracking a delimiter stack, which couples comprehension to an editor's matching and folding.

Delimiter coupling: the reader must agree with the editor on where a structure begins and ends, because the structure is carried by characters rather than by layout. The agreement is paid per reading, not per change, which is why tooling can absorb most of it.
Common Lisp's parentheses nest deeply, and the text is hard to read without an editor that matches them. Perl's sigils add a character to nearly every variable reference.
**Minor because tooling removes most of it**, and because the cost is paid once per reading rather than once per change.
The language or its standard toolchain provides no test framework, assertion, or runner. The verification of the code becomes a shared resource that each project has to build and maintain for itself.

Verification coupling: each project must agree with its own harness about what "tested" means, because the language ships no framework, assertion, or runner. The agreement is local, so a result is only as meaningful as the harness that produced it.

In Assembly a test is another program that runs and compares, and the harness lives outside the assembler. Scratch has no assertion and no runner, so a test is a manual run. Turbo Pascal ships no test framework, and neither do most shells beyond what an exit code can say.

**`G1` records what the language and its standard toolchain ship.** A mature third-party framework can remove the practical cost without changing what the language provides — which is what the criterion is about.

Finding a failure means reading machine state or log output rather than a named abstraction. The diagnosis becomes a shared resource held only by whoever can read the raw state, so debugging skill does not travel with the code.

Diagnosis coupling: whoever debugs must agree with the machine's own state about what happened, because the language offers no named abstraction over it. The agreement is personal — it exists in one practitioner's reading skill and nowhere in the code.

A debugger that exposes registers and raw memory turns a fault into a machine-state question. Haskell's laziness means the failing expression is not the one that produced the value. Zig's comptime evaluation and Unison's content-addressed code make the executed form differ from the source. Turbo Pascal's IDE steps and watches variables, with no assertion or coverage support.
**`G2` is not `G3`.** `G2` is "you cannot see what happened"; `G3` is "nothing told you beforehand".

A mistake of the kind a compiler could catch is deferred to the executed path. The correctness of an unexecuted path is then unknown, so coverage becomes the only evidence of safety — a shared resource that every contributor has to maintain.

Coverage coupling: the correctness of an unexecuted path must agree with whatever the tests happened to reach, because the compiler declined to decide it. The agreement is a property of the suite rather than of the source, so it changes when the tests change.

A wrong block in Scratch is found by running the project. A type mistake in Elixir, Erlang, Python, Ruby, JavaScript, or Perl surfaces on the path that reaches it. TypeScript's `any` re-opens the gap the language closes elsewhere. In Prolog a goal fails at run time, and in R a coercion fails when it is evaluated.

**`G3` is deliberately `T1` counted again.** The same language property costs once as coupling, under `T1`, and once as deferred verification, here. The model counts both because a program pays both — and the dimensions are separate because the remedies are separate.

The language permits access to memory outside the bounds of an object, and to storage that has already been freed. Every pointer becomes a shared resource with no owner and no bound, so a fault in one module can corrupt another module's data.

Memory-bound coupling: every pointer must agree with the object it addresses, because the language keeps no record of the bound. The agreement crosses module and trust boundaries alike, which is why a violation is an exploit rather than a defect.

In C a buffer overflow, a use-after-free, a double free, and an out-of-bounds write are all possible, and nothing in the language prevents them. In C++ the same faults compile: `reinterpret_cast`, pointer arithmetic, and manual `new`/`delete` remain available, and the standard library is safe only where a program uses it. Zig keeps manual memory management and undefined behaviour, so a use-after-free and a mistyped `@ptrCast` are reachable. In Assembly an address is a number, with no abstraction in between.

**`Q1` prices a class of *vulnerability*, and carries the top weight for it.** The others price maintainability; `Q1` prices an exploit, and any pointer suffices. `M6` prices the sibling class — type confusion — at Moderate, because it needs a pun site and a type with invariants to break.

**The safe subset is the default, or the charge stands.** A language is charged when the violation is reachable in what a new project writes without a decision. Rust and Swift are not charged: the safe subset is the default, and the unsafe paths are explicit and delimited per site. C# is not charged: `unsafe` blocks are opt in. Zig is charged: the safety checks that hold in a debug build are removed in the release build the consumer runs, so the shipped binary is the unchecked one. A flag, a lint, or a coding standard is a mitigation and never an exemption.

mechanisms.label: dynamic/weak typing risk
mechanisms.title: Dynamic or weak typing as a security risk

criteria.text: A value from an untrusted source arrives with no declared type, so keeping it away from a dangerous operation is the programmer's check. The trust boundary becomes a shared resource that the type system does not mark, so a missing check leaves no trace.

Trust-boundary coupling: a value from outside must agree with the dangerous operation it will reach, because the type system does not mark which values are trusted. The agreement is written by hand at the boundary and leaves no trace when it is missing.

In Python, Ruby, JavaScript, and PHP a request value is whatever the input made it, so a check has to be written and kept. A Prolog term carries no declared type, so a value from an untrusted source is separated from a goal only by an explicit test. In Smalltalk a type confusion is discovered at run time, so an unexecuted path stays unchecked.
**`Q2` is `Q1`'s sibling for dynamic languages.** The same missing type information costs once as coupling, under `T1` or `T2`, and once as a security surface here.

The language turns text into code or commands as an ordinary operation, so concatenated input is an injection path. The code's own text becomes a shared resource reachable from data, so a data path can become a control path.

Data-to-control coupling: text from a data path must agree with the parser that will execute it, because the language supplies conversion from text to code as a built-in operation. The agreement is available to whoever controls the text, so the boundary that matters is the input rather than the code.

PL/SQL's `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` and `DBMS_SQL` build a statement as text. R's `eval(parse(text = ...))`, `do.call` on a string, and `system()` turn text into code or into a command. A shell's `eval` sends a quoted variable back through the parser. In Transact-SQL and SQL a statement assembled by concatenation carries the caller's text. PowerShell's `Invoke-Expression` does the same.

**`Q3` records the language-level facility, not its misuse.** Parameterised queries and prepared statements are the mitigation, and the criterion is charged because the facility remains available and remains the path of least resistance.

Two builds of the same source do not produce the same artifact. The build environment — timestamps, absolute paths, file order, a random seed — becomes an input the source does not name, so the artifact is tied to the machine that made it and no third party can confirm that it matches the source.

Build-environment coupling: the artifact must agree with inputs that the source does not name — timestamps, paths, file order, a seed — because the build records them rather than normalises them. The agreement is invisible in the source and fixed at build time.

Maven, PyPI, and RubyGems packages are largely unreproducible as published, because archive metadata and build paths leak into the artifact; Cargo and npm fix those values and reach reproducible builds [@benedetti2025reproducible]; the general problem is surveyed in [@lamb2022reproducible].
**The criterion records the default of the language's own build tool**, not what a careful team can arrange.

observation.text: Builds are not byte-reproducible by default.

criteria.text: The dependency set is not pinned, so the build resolves to different versions at two points in time. The resolved graph is a shared resource that the source does not record, and the build that passed is not the build that ships.

Resolution coupling: the build must agree with the index about which versions exist, because nothing in the source fixes the answer. The agreement is made at build time and then forgotten, so two builds of one source can differ.
A Python `requirements.txt` without hashes, or a `setup.py` that names ranges, leaves the resolution to the index. Cargo's `Cargo.lock`, npm's `package-lock.json`, and Go's `go.sum` pin the graph.

observation.text: Dependencies resolve without a lock by default.

mechanisms.label: no signed provenance
mechanisms.title: No signed provenance for published packages

criteria.text: A published package carries no verifiable statement of who built it and from what source. The artifact's origin is a shared resource that the consumer must take on trust, so a compromised build is indistinguishable from a genuine one.

Origin coupling: the consumer must agree with the publisher's build, because the artifact carries no evidence of who made it or from what. The agreement rests on trust in a supply chain the consumer cannot inspect.

npm and PyPI can attach Sigstore-signed provenance, and Maven Central now validates Sigstore signatures [@sigstoreProject; @slsaSpec]. A bare checksum gives integrity against corruption, not against substitution.

**Presence is "no signing or provenance facility", not "no Sigstore".** Maven Central requires a PGP signature, npm ships registry signatures, PyPI ships TUF metadata and opt-in attestations, RubyGems and NuGet have their own signing, and Go's checksum database is a signed transparency log. A registry that offers only a bare checksum, and a language with no registry, are charged.

observation.text: Published packages carry no signed provenance by default.

criteria.text: The package registry has one flat name space and no ownership model, so a name can be claimed or confused. The name is the shared resource, and a dependency can be redirected to a different author without a change in the consumer's source.

Name-ownership coupling: the consumer must agree with whoever holds the name, because the registry records a first claim rather than an author. The agreement can be reassigned without the consumer's code changing at all.

PyPI, npm, crates.io, RubyGems, Hex, NuGet, and pub.dev reserve a flat name first-come, and npm and PyPI have both suffered dependency-confusion and typosquatting attacks. Maven Central's group coordinates, Go's module paths, CPAN's nested namespaces, SwiftPM's `scope.package-name`, and Packagist's `vendor/package` carry a namespace. **A language with no package registry is not charged**: the mechanism is about a name space that exists.

observation.text: The package registry is a flat name space.

mechanisms.label: no stable tracing standard
mechanisms.title: No stable tracing and metrics standard

criteria.text: The language and its standard library provide no agreed way to emit traces and metrics, so each project invents one. The instrumentation contract is a shared resource, and a distributed call cannot be followed across a service the project did not write.

Instrumentation-contract coupling: every service must agree with every other on a format for traces and metrics, because no standard supplies one. The agreement is invisible until a call crosses a boundary the project does not own.

OpenTelemetry ships stable tracing for C++, C#, Erlang/Elixir, Go, Java, JavaScript, PHP, Python, Ruby, and Swift, beta for Rust, and development status for Kotlin [@opentelemetryLanguages]. A language on the JVM or the CLR can use the stable Java or .NET implementation.

observation.text: No stable tracing and metrics standard.

mechanisms.label: no structured logging
mechanisms.title: No structured logging in the standard library

criteria.text: Diagnostics are free text, and the standard library exposes no structured record of them. The program's state is a shared resource held in an unstructured log, so a question about a running system requires a new deployment to answer.

Log-schema coupling: the running system must agree with whoever parses its output on a format, because the standard library records no structure. The agreement is informal and unwritten, so it breaks when a message changes.

observation.text: The standard library has no structured logging.

criteria.text: A change costs a long rebuild, and the rebuild repeats work it did not need to. The build is a shared resource on the critical path of every edit, so the feedback loop is set by the compiler rather than by the size of the change.

Feedback coupling: every edit must agree with the compiler's rebuild cost, because the build repeats work that the change did not require. The agreement is paid on every edit that ends in a build, whatever the size of the change.
A large C++ translation unit and a large Rust crate both pay a long codegen and link step. Go and a scripting language pay almost none.

observation.text: A change pays a slow build.

criteria.text: The language has no incremental analyser that answers a question about the code as it is typed. The type and reference information is a shared resource available only after a full build, so the editor cannot answer while the author is working.

Answer-latency coupling: the editor must agree with a full build about what the code means, because no incremental analyser holds the answer. The agreement arrives after the fact, so the author works without it.

The language has no in-process foreign-function interface: a library written in another language is reachable only by starting a process or through an external binding. Every library must be reimplemented in the language, so the program is coupled to the ecosystem of one language and cannot reuse the rest. This is the mirror of `T14`: `T14` prices an unchecked boundary, and `Y9` prices the absence of one.

Ecosystem-reach coupling: the program must agree to live inside one language's library supply, because no in-process path reaches another language. The agreement is with a community rather than with a component, so a library choice cannot renegotiate it.

A shell reaches another language only by starting a process. Scratch, Solidity, and Rocq reach none. SQL is not charged: PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server each load native code through a user-defined function (`LANGUAGE C`, `extproc`, SQLCLR).
The program cannot be compiled to a portable target, so it runs only where the language's own runtime runs. The deployment surface is a shared resource fixed by the runtime.

Deployment-target coupling: the program's reach must agree with the runtime's reach, because the language compiles only to its own execution environment. The agreement is fixed by the implementation, so a new target is a new implementation rather than a new build flag.
Popcorn and AtomVM compile Erlang and Elixir to WebAssembly; GHC, `wasm_of_ocaml`, Pyodide, `php-wasm`, `webR`, and SwiftWasm cover their languages. Julia has no maintained official target.

One company decides the language's direction, and no independent body can change it. The language's future is a shared resource held by a commercial owner, so the program's roadmap follows that owner's priorities.

Roadmap coupling: the program's future must agree with one owner's priorities, because no independent body can change the language's direction. The agreement runs one way — the program adapts to the owner's schedule, never the reverse.

MATLAB, SAS, PL/SQL, Transact-SQL, Objective-C, Delphi, and VBScript are governed by one vendor, and Swift's project lead is appointed by Apple. Rust, Python, JavaScript, PHP, Kotlin, C#, and Eiffel sit with an independent foundation or a standards body.

observation.text: One vendor decides the language's direction.

criteria.text: The language has no public, complete definition that an independent implementation could follow. The meaning of a program is a shared resource held by one implementation, so portability and third-party tooling depend on reverse engineering.

Specification coupling: the program must agree with one implementation's behaviour, because there is no public definition to agree with instead. The agreement is discovered by experiment, and third-party tooling is built on the same experiment.
ISO C, ISO SQL, Ada, Fortran, and Scheme have published standards. MATLAB, SAS, PL/SQL, Transact-SQL, and Objective-C do not.

mechanisms.label: no conformance mechanism
mechanisms.title: Correctness Is What the Dominant Implementation Does

criteria.text: The language's meaning lives in the behavior of the dominant implementation. The vendor's documentation describes what the shipped toolchain does; implementation-defined corners are not enumerated as a list; and no published conformance suite exists for an independent implementation to run. A program's correctness is then a toolchain property, not a language property: the only oracle of what the code means is the compiler everyone already ships.

Conformance coupling: every consumer of the language's semantics depends on one implementation's choices, documented after the fact. The agreement is between the program and a toolchain nobody can test independently, so a second implementation is a compatibility gamble, a bug in the dominant one becomes the language's behavior, and the code has no external standard to return to.

The C standard lists its implementation-defined behaviors (J.2) and the NCAR suite runs against independent compilers, so C is not charged. Java marks implementation-defined corners in the JLS, and the conformance kit runs against every licensed implementation. Haskell publishes a test suite that independent implementations run. Against these: Perl, Clojure, Erlang, and Elixir are documented as the behavior of their implementations, and no published conformance suite exists; C++ lists its implementation-defined behavior in the standard and the committee publishes no suite; MATLAB, R, Julia, SAS, ABAP, X++, Scratch, and GML document the semantics of the product the vendor ships.

**`Y12` prices the closed specification; this prices the open one with no checkable core.** `Y12` charges a specification that is not public. This mechanism charges a public document whose semantics rest on the dominant implementation, with no enumerated implementation-defined list and no published conformance suite for an independent implementation to run. Both are governance facts; the first closes the document, this one leaves the oracle a single toolchain.

**`V4` prices the standard moving glacially; this prices no standard testable at all.** A language can have a published standard with a slow committee (`V4`) and still ship a conformance suite — C does. A language can have no committee at all and a published suite — JavaScript ships Test262. The two facts are independent, and this mechanism charges only the second absence.

**A development suite is not a conformance suite.** A repository's tests validate the reference implementation's own behavior; they are run by maintainers, not by independent implementations, and they do not settle the unspecified corners. The mechanism charges when no published suite exists for an independent implementation to run against the language's semantics. The published suites that settle it: Test262 (JavaScript), the TCK (Java), ACVS (Ada), the NIST suites (C, COBOL, SQL, Fortran-77), the R6RS and ANSI-CL test suites, the Haskell Test Suite, the Go suite that gccgo runs, the CLI conformance suite behind C# and VB.NET.

**Context, not language.** The tag says where the remedy lives: the vendor's governance of its own specification, not the programmer's code. A language family inheriting a parent's conformance mechanism inherits this verdict from the parent: the JVM languages carry Java's answer, the .NET languages carry the CLI suite, the BEAM languages share the BEAM's status, and the shells follow POSIX's scope for sh-family shells and the absence of any standard for the rest.

mechanisms.label: no bundled debugger
mechanisms.title: No debugger in the standard toolchain

criteria.text: The language's official toolchain ships no source-level debugger, so a failing run is examined by reading the source and adding print statements. The procedure for inspecting a running program is a shared resource held outside the distribution, and each team assembles it for itself.

Diagnosis coupling: every failure must be reconstructed from the source and the logs, because the toolchain cannot stop the program and show its state. The team agrees with whichever external debugger it installs, and no file in the repository records that agreement.
Python ships `pdb`, Java ships `jdb`, and Ruby bundles `debug`; Go ships no debugger and points to delve, C and C++ leave it to `gdb` or `lldb`, and PHP leaves it to Xdebug.

**Presence is the official distribution.** A commercial IDE with a debugger does not lift the charge: the criterion asks what the language itself installs, because that is what every new team starts from.

observation.text: The standard toolchain ships no debugger.

mechanisms.label: no toolchain version pin
mechanisms.title: No toolchain version pin in the official distribution

criteria.text: The official distribution offers no way to record the language's own version in the repository, so a repeatable environment needs a third-party version manager or a container image. The compiler version is a shared resource that no file in the project names.
Toolchain-version coupling: every machine and every build agent agree on a compiler version that the repository never states, so the agreement is rebuilt by memory or hidden inside a container image.

Rust records the toolchain in `rust-toolchain.toml` through rustup, Go records it in the `toolchain` directive of `go.mod`, .NET records it in `global.json`, and Lean records it in `lean-toolchain`; Python, Ruby, Node.js, and Java leave it to pyenv, rbenv, nvm, and SDKMAN.
**A container image is not a pin.** The dependency set may be pinned while the compiler that built it is not, and the repository still names no version that a reader can check.

observation.text: The distribution records no per-project toolchain version.

mechanisms.label: no post-mortem diagnostics
mechanisms.title: No crash or post-mortem diagnostics by default

criteria.text: A failed run leaves no stack trace with source locations and no post-mortem artifact, so a failure in production cannot be reconstructed after the fact. The state at the moment of failure is a shared resource that the runtime discards.

Post-mortem coupling: the incident must be reproduced before it can be understood, because the runtime keeps no record of where the program stopped. Reproduction depends on an environment that has already changed.

Python, Java, Go, C#, JavaScript, and Ruby print a stack trace with source locations on an unhandled failure; C and C++ print nothing without a debugger and an enabled core dump; Rust prints a backtrace only when `RUST_BACKTRACE` is set, and OCaml only when `OCAMLRUNPARAM=b` is set.
**A trace that only a special build produces is not present.** The criterion asks what an ordinary build does when it fails, because that is the build that runs in production.

observation.text: A failure leaves no stack trace or post-mortem artifact.

mechanisms.label: no advisory feed
mechanisms.title: No vulnerability advisory feed for dependencies

criteria.text: The ecosystem maintains no advisory database joined to package versions, so a known vulnerability in a dependency is found by reading release notes or by a scanner that guesses. The vulnerability state of the dependency set is a shared resource that no feed records.

Advisory coupling: every consumer must track the vulnerability state of its own dependency graph, because no shared feed joins an advisory to the versions it affects. Each team builds the same map, and the maps disagree.

OSV and the GitHub Advisory Database cover npm, PyPI, Maven, NuGet, RubyGems, Packagist, Cargo, Go, Hex, Pub, and Swift; CPAN, Hackage, CRAN, the Julia General registry, LuaRocks, and dub have no equivalent maintained feed.
**A scanner without an advisory database is not a feed.** A tool that reports what a registry's metadata implies does not record a vulnerability that a maintainer disclosed somewhere else.

observation.text: No advisory feed joins vulnerabilities to package versions.
